$4.6 trillion. Zero growth from the year before.

That's how Staffing Industry Analysts values the Americas' contingent workforce in 2025 — contractors, consultants, statement-of-work engagements, temporary talent — in its Americas Contingent Workforce 2026 report (published August 2026, authored by SIA Senior Research Director Adam Pode). The US accounts for $4 trillion of that total. Read on its own, that looks like a market that stalled.

One number underneath it says otherwise: Google searches for "contingent workforce" were nearly 10x higher in July 2026 than in January 2025, per the same report.

Worth naming upfront: SIA's members are staffing and workforce-solutions firms, so research showing flexible work growing in importance also serves their business. The numbers come from a large, longstanding industry analyst firm rather than a single vendor's own platform data, which makes this more reliable than most vendor surveys — just not fully neutral either.

Pode's own read lines up with the search spike: AI, persistent skills shortages and more uncertainty are changing how organizations think about workforce capacity. He describes contingent talent as becoming less a tactical response to demand spikes and more a strategic part of workforce planning.

The mix inside that flat $4.6 trillion backs that up. Statement-of-work engagements now make up 73.3% of contingent workforce revenue — the largest category — and grew by roughly $30 billion this year even as the total held flat. Independent contractors are the second-largest category, at 16.5%.

Three things worth taking from this if you source any mix of permanent and flexible talent:

1. Rising demand for flexible talent is often a faster way to access a specific AI or data skill an organization isn't ready to hire for permanently — not only a cost-cutting move.

2. Vetting a statement-of-work engagement or a consulting firm is a different skill than screening an individual candidate. The deliverable is what you're actually evaluating, not a resume.

3. A flat market-size number can hide a real shift happening inside it. Check what's growing underneath the headline total before assuming nothing changed.

Is flexible or contract talent becoming a bigger part of how your organization closes a skills gap, or is permanent hiring still the only lever anyone reaches for?

AI-written code is already in production at many engineering teams. In a lot of them, so is the first outage it caused.

A March 2026 Censuswide survey of 500 US IT engineers and engineering leaders found 89% of their organisations have had at least one AI-related production incident, and 25% an outage caused by AI-generated code.

The speed gain is real. So is the bill when review, tests and incident tracking are still sized for code written at human typing speed. An outage costs revenue by the hour, and the fix eats the sprint the speed was supposed to buy.

Three checks worth running before AI-written code merges:
1. Does every AI-written change go through the same tests and review as a human one, in changes small enough to actually review?
2. Do your incident reviews record whether the change was AI-written?
3. Who on the team is senior enough to catch what an AI-written change gets wrong, and do they have time to review it?

The third one is often a hiring question. Squad XP places senior engineers into product teams on a monthly retainer or contract-to-hire.

Most businesses don’t have an AI tool problem. They have an execution gap.
Over the last few weeks speaking with independent coaches, training academies, and consulting founders, the same pattern keeps coming up:
They don’t want another disconnected subscription. And they certainly don’t want a long, rigid software contract before seeing if it actually works for their clients.
Whether you run a solo practice or a corporate training and consulting firm, the rule is simple:
Start with one real bottleneck — missed inquiries, slow WhatsApp follow-ups, manual hiring screening, or scattered course delivery.
Run a focused pilot first — prove the workflow saves time or converts leads before scaling.
Keep everything connected — discovery, landing pages, AI assistants, and client follow-up in one place instead of 6 separate logins.
When you test the outcome first, AI stops being an experiment and starts paying for itself.
If you could automate just one bottleneck in your practice or firm this month, what would it be?

Most AI advice tells you what it can do. The useful question is what it should do.

After years running my own business, here's the matrix I use.

First: is it worth it?

Time per task × how often × what that time costs.

A 5-minute task done 200 times a month beats a 3-hour task done once a quarter.

Then two questions:

- What does a mistake cost?

- Can you easily check the output?

→ Cheap, easy to check: Automate it. Scheduling, invoicing, data entry.

→ Costly, easy to check: AI drafts, you sign off. Contracts, pricing, customer comms.

→ Cheap, hard to check: Use it, spot-check. Research, competitor scans.

→ Costly, hard to check: Keep it human. Hiring, key clients, crisis calls.

But the matrix misses one thing: the relationship.

Sending invoices? Automate it. Chasing an overdue one from a client you know? Pick up the phone. A real call gets you paid faster than any AI reminder ever will.

Before you hand anything over, ask: does a human relationship make this work?

The mistake I see most often isn't using too little AI. It's using it in the wrong box.

Which task would you never hand to AI? 👇

A trading house just spun out a software company. A Tier-1 is buying 20% of it.

Read that twice. Toyota Tsusho moves materials and parts around the world. It's not the name you expect behind in-vehicle code.

On November 16 it announced Toyota Tsusho Definex. The company was set up in September and starts operations in January 2027.

The detail that matters: this isn't new. For 20+ years, Toyota Tsusho has done contract development of in-vehicle software through its subsidiary NEXTY Electronics. It also ran a software distribution platform and standards work. A side business that quietly grew up.

Now it's carved out as its own company. Toyota Tsusho holds 80%. DENSO is expected to take 20%.

Why would DENSO, with its own software army, buy in?

Because code grew faster than hiring. Both companies say it plainly. In-vehicle software keeps growing in scale and complexity, and specialized talent is the bottleneck. No single org chart is deep enough anymore.

So it's a trade. Tsusho brings development capacity and business design. DENSO brings mass-production discipline and quality. The pitch is an "Engineering Service Provider" for the hard parts of in-vehicle software, with AI in the workflow.

There's also moderix, a platform to distribute software assets, designed with AI-driven development in mind. Reuse, turned into a product.

After 20 years of watching programs slip at integration, here's my read. The scarce resource in SDV isn't ideas. It's engineers who have shipped through ASIL and ASPICE gates, and who know a release isn't done until it survives a real vehicle.

Capacity is now being organized into companies, not just teams.

Who in your ecosystem is building the bench, not just the roadmap?

I’m a solo ABS and MSO lawyer, and this year, I built my own client management system with Claude.

It beats the vendor software I was paying for. Yet, my firm is STILL not AI-native.

Let me back up. When ChatGPT launched, I was obviously hesitant. Everyone was talking about it and I couldn’t figure out what it did well. 

What finally got me? A colleague planned an entire Japan trip with it in one afternoon. Restaurants, trains, neighborhoods I’d never heard of. I downloaded the app that night.

Fast forward, and I’m building my own software for my firm and I'm not an engineer. But here’s the thing.

That’s AI-enabled. Not AI-native.

An AI-enabled firm uses tools. Research goes faster. Contract review goes faster. But folks still tend to bill by the hour, still need a partner reviewing every associate’s work and still grow by hiring. Same firm, just faster.

I’d wager that’s most firms. (To an extent, mine included.)

An AI-native firm asks a much harder question: if you were building a legal services business TODAY, knowing what AI can do, what would you build?

It’s easier to hand out Harvey subscriptions and call it a year. I get it.

But for a lot of people who can’t afford a lawyer, the answer to that question decides whether they get one at all.

Your healthcare AI startup could save clinicians hundreds of hours and still lose the contract because you haven't saved the hospital a single dollar. This came up again today, so I'm posting this.

This is one of the most expensive commercial mistakes I see healthcare AI founders make.

They calculate hours saved, multiply them by clinician salaries and call it ROI.

For example, if your AI saves 1,000 clinician hours at an average loaded cost of $150 per hour, you claim $150,000 in savings.

1,000 hours × $150 = $150,000.

The founder sees $150,000 in savings.

The CFO sees $150,000 in theoretical productivity and absolutely nothing coming off the payroll.

Your pitch deck says $150,000 saved.

The hospital's P&L says $0.

And the CFO has one question.

"Which line on my P&L actually changes?"

If you can't answer that, your ROI calculation is worthless as evidence of financial savings.
Unless those hours reduce overtime, avoid additional hires or generate profitable patient encounters, you haven't demonstrated a financial return.

You've demonstrated time saved.

And that's the difference between a product clinicians love and a contract the CFO will actually approve.

Your clinical champion loves the product. The pilot works. But without a credible financial return, your successful pilot risks becoming another stalled contract.

So here's what I'd recommend.

Before starting a pilot, agree with the CFO on a measurable financial outcome.

Establish the baseline and track actual reductions in overtime or agency spending, avoided hiring costs, or additional contribution margin from increased patient volume.

Subtract software, implementation, training and ongoing operating costs.

Now you've got a credible basis for calculating financial ROI.

Clinical productivity matters. Better working conditions matter. Giving clinicians more time with patients matters.

But those benefits aren't automatically financial savings.

And if your entire commercial proposition depends on savings that never materialize, you don't have a product performance problem.

You have a business model that may not survive procurement.

No amount of AI innovation will fix a commercial proposition built on financial returns the customer cannot realize.

Your team just shipped a new AI feature. If it goes wrong, who is legally on the hook?
Most leaders answer “the vendor.” Under the EU AI Act, that’s only sometimes true. Your responsibility depends on the role you play, and that role can change because of a product decision, not a legal one.

The roles, in plain terms:

Provider. The one who builds the AI system, or has it built, and sells it under its own name. This carries the heavy obligations: risk management, technical documentation, testing, conformity checks.

Deployer. The one who uses an AI system in its own business. The job is to use it as intended, keep a human overseeing it, monitor it, keep logs, and tell people when AI affects them.

Importer and distributor. The ones who bring a system to market or pass it along, and verify the paperwork first.

Most companies start as deployers, which is a comfortable place to be. But Article 25 moves you into the provider seat if you:

1. Put your own brand on a high-risk AI system
2. Substantially modify a high-risk system
3. Change a system’s purpose so that it becomes high-risk

Here’s what that looks like in real life. A company takes a general-purpose chatbot, adds its own branding, and offers it to clients to screen job candidates. Nobody signed anything. Nobody announced anything. But hiring is a high-risk use, so that company now carries the provider’s obligations, and the fines for getting it wrong can reach 15 million euros or 3% of global turnover.

Two things to know. A contract with your vendor can split responsibility, but it can’t remove what the law requires of you. And the original provider has to cooperate, but you have to ask.

Three questions for your next leadership meeting:
1. Which AI systems do we use, and what role do we play for each?
2. Have we rebranded, modified, or repurposed any of them?
3. Who in the company would notice if our role changed?
It’s a short conversation today. It’s a very long one after an incident.

📌 The most famous job in cinema just went to a man who has already carried two global franchises.

At 15:00 GMT on Monday 16 November 2026, Amazon MGM Studios named Robert Pattinson, 40, as the next 007.

✅ What is confirmed:
- He is the seventh actor in the official series and will lead the 26th film, directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight (Amazon MGM Studios)
- It is the first Bond film since Amazon MGM took creative control in 2025. Amazon bought MGM in 2022 for about $8.45bn (CNBC)
- No title or release date has been announced (CNBC)
- The casting search was announced in May 2026 (BBC)

❓ What is not confirmed: his contract. Puck reported fewer films and higher pay than rival candidates. Amazon declined to comment.

🟢 Twilight films: more than $3bn worldwide
🔵 The Batman: $773m
🟠 All 25 official Bond films: $7.8bn

From making a star to hiring one.
From betting on potential to paying for proof.
From "who could grow into this?" to "who has already done it?"

⚖️ The tension: Bond used to do the building. Christopher Hogg of the University of Westminster, quoted by Deadline, said no earlier Bond was this famous before taking the role. He also noted that Daniel Craig's casting was criticised early and then succeeded.

🤖 Why this matters for CEOs and CFOs over the next ten years:
AI is absorbing the entry-level tasks where people used to prove themselves. So employers do what Amazon did: pay a premium for a verified track record. Rational for one hire. Risky for an economy, because proven talent has to be unproven somewhere first.

📒 The audit principle still holds: evidence beats promise. But someone has to give people the chance to create the evidence.

🔮 My forecast: by the end of 2030, Amazon MGM's next Bond lead, in any film or series, will also have fronted a global franchise already.

❌ What would prove me wrong: Amazon MGM gives that lead to a relative unknown, or names no one by 31 December 2030.

3. Who owns our talent pipeline, and what will it have produced by 2030?

💡 Proof is priced at a premium. Somebody still has to fund the first chance.

4 ways to build a product on a limited budget (as a non-technical manager)

AI dramatically changed the way we build software. But that doesn’t make it free.

If you are a non-technical manager trying to build an internal tool or an MVP, here are the 4 setups I see most often and their trade-offs.

1. Vibe-code it yourself

When you’re willing to get your hands dirty.

- Upside: The cheapest option if you have spare time
- Downside: Steep learning curve. You’ll spend dozens of hours figuring out how to set everything up and you’re still likely to mess up the codebase past the point of recovery.

2. Contract a mid-level dev full-time

When ‘merging a PR’ sounds like a magic spell to you and you’d rather keep it that way.

- Upside: Frees you completely from technical details
- Downside: He’ll end up acting as an AI operator on your behalf. Without senior architectural judgment he’ll accept whatever AI throws at him resulting in endless back-and-forth and a buggy implementation.

3. Contract a senior-level dev part-time to build stuff

When you still want to delegate, but you’re tired of constant rework and want a seasoned approach

- Upside: Less back-and-forth and rework, maintainable code
- Downside: Progress can feel like watching a pot boil

4. Vibe-code + consult a senior-level dev

When you want to build it yourself, but keep getting stuck in endless rework loops.

- Upside: You still get to be the builder with someone to stop you from digging yourself an architectural grave.
- Downside: Slower pace. Still need to learn the basics of CI/CD, testing and system design.


The verdict

Building software on a limited budget is always a compromise.

But here is my take: I see little value in hiring a full-time mid-level dev on a small-scale project.

You’re better off hiring a part-time experienced dev who actually knows how to design the system, set up the foundation and enforce the best engineering practices.

If you’re willing to spend time and learn how to build a product yourself then consulting with a seasoned dev pays off in the long run.

I just onboarded a new team member. It isn't human.

In 2026, businesses are hiring AI agents that send emails, book appointments and move money. Most companies wouldn't let a new human hire do any of that without a job description, a manager and a probation period.

That's roughly where things stand: 54% of companies are running AI agents in production or actively piloting them, but only 25% consistently measure the impact of their AI agents using defined KPIs. Deloitte found only 21% of organizations report having mature governance models for agentic AI. 

As a law student candidate, here's what caught my attention. Courts are starting to apply agency law, the centuries-old rules for when someone acts on your behalf. In one case, the court held Workday's software acted as an agent. Legal analysts point out that agency law assumes a principal can direct its agent's conduct, yet agentic AI can take emergent, unforeseeable actions no human specifically authorized.  

So I treat every AI agent like a new hire, using what I call The Agent Employee File:

📋 Job description: the exact tasks it owns, and nothing more.
🔑 Scope of authority: what it can do alone, and what needs a human's sign-off (spending limits, external emails, contracts).
👤 Manager of record: one named human who is accountable for it.
📊 Performance review: KPIs checked every 30 days.
🧾 Paper trail: logs of what it did and why.
🚪 Offboarding: how to shut it off and take back its access.

The companies that win with AI won't necessarily be the ones with the most agents. They'll be the ones that can explain what their agents did.

The conventional narrative around AWS in 2026 is that it's playing defense against Azure and GCP. I think that misses the point entirely. The real story is how AWS is quietly weaponizing its legacy complexity into a moat for enterprise workloads.

The most underappreciated move this year is not the AI models on Bedrock. It's the operational unification of observability and cost management. AWS is no longer just selling compute and storage. It is selling a control plane for the entire lifecycle of a workload, from development to decommissioning, with native cost attribution baked in. This is the kind of integration that makes it nearly impossible to migrate a mature system to Azure or GCP without rebuilding your entire FinOps model from scratch.

Consider the practical implication for a mid-stage startup or a legacy enterprise: when your cost allocation tags, your CloudWatch dashboards, your IAM policies, and your AI inference all live inside the same VPC boundary, you can audit a production failure in minutes instead of days. The engineering advantage here is not speed of deployment. It is speed of diagnosis.

The second shift I find compelling is the evolution of EventBridge as a central bus for not just events, but for state. Most teams still treat EventBridge as a simple pub/sub pipe. But with the latest schema registry improvements and the ability to enforce event contracts via CDK, you can now model complex business processes as declarative event flows. This moves us closer to a world where your infrastructure actually enforces your business logic, not the other way around.

For hiring managers who need someone who can navigate this: I do not chase the newest service announcement. I build systems that leverage the full depth of the AWS ecosystem to reduce operational noise. If your team is drowning in cross-account complexity, struggling with cost attribution for AI workloads, or fighting event storms without a clear recovery strategy, I bring the architectural discipline to simplify it.

What is the one operational pain point on AWS that you have accepted as inevitable, but you suspect there is a better way to solve?

A friend called me this morning. He was worried. 
His software company is losing business because clients are cutting vendor contracts, convinced they can now build everything in-house with AI.

I reminded him of what happened in Silicon Valley a few years ago.

Major technology companies laid off thousands of engineers, only to discover later that they still needed some of that expertise and start hiring again.

I suspect we're about to see a similar cycle with enterprise AI.

Because pulling off the AI trick requires two jokers up your sleeve: 

Joker 1. people who actually understand your business.

AI can read your entire codebase.

It can analyze years of documentation and explain how your systems work.

But that doesn't mean it understands why they work that way.

Why Finance insisted on that strange approval process.

Why one distributor gets treated differently, etc. 

Much of that knowledge lives inside people's heads.

And some of those people are precisely the ones companies are thinking about replacing.

Joker 2. AI-native engineers who know how to work together.

This is where things get even more complicated.

Giving ten engineers access to coding agents doesn't magically create an agentic delivery organization.

You need people with serious AI engineering experience who can operate as one team. And, believe me, achieving even one of these conditions is an uphill battle for most non-technical companies.  

Oh.. and those engineers they need a common framework.
One that preserves context as requirements change, coordinates work across departments, enforces engineering standards and makes sure the software being delivered still solves the business problem.

Even traditional engineering organizations struggle with this kind of coordination.

And here we're talking about introducing dozens of agents that can produce code faster than your team can review it.

It already sounds complicated. 
But I'm barely scratching the surface.

And yet I'm watching companies reduce their engineering resources because they've convinced themselves AI will somehow handle the rest.

I think that's a very expensive misunderstanding.

AI can dramatically reduce the amount of human effort required to build software.

But the expertise needed to direct that work, understand the business and take responsibility for the result becomes even more valuable.

Want a simpler version? 

Let's say I gave you a brand new helicopter. It's parked on your back yard. 

And there's a zombie apocalypse tomorrow. 

Flying your family out is the only option. 

Will you give it a blind try just because you know how drive a car? Or will you look for a professional pilot? 

Exactly.. except you might have fired yours.
